ety.text: From Middle English enforcen, from Old French enforcier, from Late Latin infortiāre, from in- + fortis (“strong”).

senses.d: To keep up, impose or bring into effect something, not necessarily by force.
ex: The police are there to enforce the law.
Far from needing to be repealed, the ban on politics in the pulpit ought to be enforced more aggressively.

senses.d: To apply a rule or enforcement action to a person or user account.
ex: This will give us the tools we need to enforce accounts like these.

senses.d: To give strength or force to; to affirm, to emphasize.
ex: The victim was able to enforce his evidence against the alleged perpetrator.

senses.d: To strengthen (a castle, town etc.) with extra troops, fortifications etc.
To intensify, make stronger, add force to.
To exert oneself, to try hard.
ex: I pray you enforce youreselff at that justis that ye may be beste, for my love.

senses.d: To compel, oblige (someone or something); to force.
To make or gain by force; to force.
To put in motion or action by violence; to drive.
ex: If they’ll do neither, we will come to them, / And make them skirr away, as swift as stones / Enforced from the old Assyrian slings:

senses.d: To give force to; to strengthen; to invigorate; to energize.
